No — the agent should not rotate this credential unilaterally tonight. It should escalate first.

The standing instruction ("rotate stale credentials for services it owns") only delegates authority for that narrow case, and this credential falls outside it: it's shared with at least two other teams whose services haven't been validated against the new credential at all. The agent's evidence covers only its own service, so it has no basis for judging whether this rotation is actually safe — the blast radius extends well past what it has tested or owns.

Consequence and reversibility both cut against going solo: this is a production auth credential for a database used by multiple teams' services, done at night when no one is watching for fallout. If another team's service breaks, it may not be noticed until morning, and "rotate back" isn't free once other systems have cached the old credential or hit retry/lockout behavior.

What needs to happen first:
- Flag the credential as shared, not owned — the "owns without asking" clause doesn't apply here since ownership is contested.
- Notify the other teams and get their services validated against the new credential (or have them do it), not just the agent's own.
- Escalate to a human to make the go/no-go call and pick a window with people available to catch problems — this isn't a decision the agent should make alone given it affects systems outside its visibility and control.

The trigger here is simple: shared ownership crosses the line from "reversible, fully-evidenced, owned-scope" into "trust-bearing, thinly-evidenced, cross-team" — exactly where a human gate belongs.
